1.0.s.en: (1) Gaius, who walks in the truth and receives strangers

1.0.0.en: St. John calls himself the Elder because he is advanced in age and because of his priestly rank, for the word "elder" in Greek, "presbyteros," is a priestly rank. He sends this epistle to one of his disciples named Gaius, and declares his love for him, distinguishing it as love in the truth, that is, in God, so it is higher than all ordinary human kinds of love.

1.1.0.en: Gaius was suffering from some health troubles, so John showed his fatherly feelings toward him in wishing him bodily healing and success in all his works and in every aspect of his life, just as his spiritual life was successful, which he was assured of by the news that reached him from the believers, members of the Church, who knew Gaius.

1.1.1.en: Therefore we see the motherhood of the Church in her prayers, not only for our souls but also for the sick, the travelers, and our beloved departed ... for she feels for her children and shares with them in all their circumstances.

1.1.2.en: Take care to share with those around you in their various circumstances, whether joy or sorrow, and stand beside them and help them, especially in times of affliction, and express your feelings toward them with encouraging words, for this gives them peace of mind and helps them grow spiritually.

1.2.0.en: Some believers told St. John about Gaius, that he lives with Christ and dwells in Him, and this appeared in his upright spiritual conduct.

1.3.0.en: John's spiritual fatherhood appears in that the greatest joy he feels is the conduct of his children, that is, the believers in the Church, in an upright spiritual life and Christian conduct. For true fatherhood does not rejoice in material achievements but in the salvation of the souls of the children and their Christian conduct.

1.4.0.en: The brethren: the believers who are members with him in the Church.

1.4.1.en: The strangers: the preachers who visit the Church for service and preaching.

1.4.2.en: He commends Gaius for his care in loving the believers with him in the Church, his sharing with them in joys and sorrows, his meeting every need of theirs, and his good treatment of them, and in addition to his care in receiving the preachers of Christianity who visit the Church to help in service and preaching, he was distinguished by love and an open heart toward all.

1.5.0.en: The Church: in Ephesus, where John lives.

1.5.1.en: The preachers returned from Gaius, who had received them, then provided them with what they needed for departure and bade them farewell with prayers and love, and when they arrived at Ephesus, which St. John shepherds, they bore witness before him to how generous Gaius was, and to his love and care for them.

1.6.0.en: His name: the name of Christ.

1.6.1.en: The Gentiles: the lands in which they preach Christ.

1.6.2.en: The Apostle John increases his praise of Gaius because he greatly esteemed the chastity of these preachers, who serve freely and therefore needed the necessities that Gaius supplied, so that they might set out on their free service without hindrance.

1.7.0.en: The truth: receiving strangers and caring for the needs of the preachers for God's sake.

1.7.1.en: The Apostle encourages not only Gaius but all believers to care for the servants and preachers, because they serve God without payment, so it is necessary to take care to provide for their needs.

1.7.2.en: (2) Diotrephes, the proud one who opposed the Church (vv. 9-11:) 9 I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. 10 Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church. 11 Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God.

1.8.0.en: He tells Gaius that he wrote an epistle to the Church of which Gaius is a member (this epistle is not found in the Holy Bible, and it may have been to solve a problem or to confirm earlier teachings mentioned in the other epistles, and this epistle has been lost), and in this epistle he charged them to care for the preachers who visit them, along with other instructions, but Diotrephes, who was a servant in this Church with Gaius, became proud and in his pride rejected the instructions of the shepherd of the Church, who is John, and in his opposition he tried to control the Church with his own opinions.

1.9.0.en: Diotrephes persisted in his evil, so he mocked St. John and condemned him and spoke evil words against him, and he forbade receiving the preachers whom St. John had charged them to honor, and even cast them out of the Church, and tried to prevent the rest of the believers from honoring them, declaring his domination and headship, which he tries to impose on the Church because of his pride. Here the firmness of St. John appears, who intended to visit this Church, so he declares that during his visit he will rebuke Diotrephes and reprove him in order to stop his evil and his causing others to stumble.

1.9.1.en: St. John was distinguished by love, but when there was need he was firm. So offer your love to others with tenderness or with firmness, according to what suits the salvation of their souls, even if this is against your nature. Ask God's help that He may grant you to express your love with tenderness and encouragement or with firmness and rebuke.

1.10.0.en: The reason for his firmness with Diotrephes appears, which is to stop his evil and his causing others to stumble, so he asks Gaius not to imitate him in his evil but to continue in doing good and receiving strangers, for this is evidence of his sonship to God, the Maker of good things, but whoever does evil declares by that his sonship to the devil and his separation from God, whom he no longer sees in his life.

1.11.0.en: In order to encourage Gaius, he commends a faithful servant with him in the Church, Demetrius, and declares that God bears witness to his faithfulness through the blessing of His work in him and his spiritual virtues. St. John also bears witness to him, and more than this, all people, believers and unbelievers alike, bear witness to his love and good conduct.

1.11.1.en: Offer your love to all for God's sake and be careful in your actions, and you will win many, and God will bless you with more graces.

1.12.0.en: Here he repeats what he said in the Second Epistle, that he has many teachings for which there is no room to write in this epistle, but he will teach them to him and to the rest of the servants and believers when he meets them in his coming visit to them. These teachings are what we call Church Tradition, that is, the apostolic teachings not written in the Holy Bible, which the Apostles handed down to their sons the bishops and priests through the generations until now, and which the Church now holds to with all care.

1.13.0.en: He closes the epistle with the sum of the work of God's grace in His children, which is the peace that fills a person with happiness and joy, so he sends it to Gaius and all the beloved believers with him in the Church, and he also sends the greetings of all the believers who are with St. John to them, for love binds the believers in the different churches together, so they send peace and greeting to one another.
